prompt: Show that there is no arithmetic progression with three elements in the infinite geometric sequence $\{2^k\}_{k=0}^\infty$.
answer: If $2^k<2^l<2^m$ were in arithmetic progression, then $2^{l+1}=2^k+2^m$, i.e. $2^{l+1-k}=1+2^{m-k}$ — an odd number $\ge 3$ equal to a power of $2$, impossible.

solutions.title: Parity after dividing by the smallest power
solutions.body:
Suppose three distinct terms of the sequence form an arithmetic progression. Order them by size: $2^k<2^l<2^m$ with $0\le k<l<m$ integers. In an arithmetic progression of three numbers the middle one is the average of the other two, so
$$2\cdot 2^l=2^k+2^m,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad 2^{l+1}=2^k\left(1+2^{m-k}\right).$$
Divide by $2^k$:
$$2^{\,l+1-k}=1+2^{\,m-k}.$$
Since $m-k\ge 2$, the right-hand side is an odd integer $\ge 5$. The left-hand side is a power of $2$ that is an integer $>1$ (because $l+1-k\ge 2$), hence even. An even number cannot equal an odd one — contradiction.

So no three terms of $\{2^k\}$ form an arithmetic progression. ∎

solutions.title: Size comparison
solutions.body:
With $0\le k<l<m$ as above we would need $2^{l+1}=2^k+2^m$. But $l+1\le m$, so
$$2^{l+1}\le 2^m<2^k+2^m ,$$
a contradiction. (The largest term alone is already at least twice the middle one, so the middle term cannot be the average.) ∎

prompt:
Compute the determinant
$$\det\begin{pmatrix}0&a_{12}&a_{13}&\dots&a_{1n}\\-a_{12}&0&a_{23}&\dots&a_{2n}\\-a_{13}&-a_{23}&0&\dots&a_{3n}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\-a_{1n}&-a_{2n}&-a_{3n}&\dots&0\end{pmatrix},$$
where $n$ is an odd number.

solutions.title: Transpose versus negation
solutions.body:
Call the matrix $A$ and let $d=\det A$. The matrix is **skew-symmetric**: $A^T=-A$.

* Multiplying every one of the $n$ rows by $-1$ multiplies the determinant by $(-1)^n=-1$ (as $n$ is odd), so $\det(-A)=-d$.
* A matrix and its transpose have the same determinant, so $\det(-A)=\det(A^T)=\det A=d$.

Hence $d=-d$, so $d=0$.

**Answer: $0$** ∎

solutions.title: Check on the $3	imes 3$ case
solutions.body:
For $n=3$, expanding directly,
$$\det\begin{pmatrix}0&a&b\\-a&0&c\\-b&-c&0\end{pmatrix}=0\cdot(0+c^2)-a\,(0+bc)+b\,(ac-0)=-abc+abc=0,$$
in agreement with the general argument (which works for every odd $n$; for even $n$ the determinant is in general nonzero, e.g. $\det\begin{pmatrix}0&a\\-a&0\end{pmatrix}=a^2$).

**Answer: $0$**

prompt:
Let $[x]$ be the integer part of $x$. Find the limit
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\Big((\sqrt3+1)^n-\big[(\sqrt3+1)^n\big]\Big).$$

solutions.title: Pair with the conjugate
solutions.body:
Let $\alpha=\sqrt3+1$ and $\beta=\sqrt3-1\in(0,1)$. Write $\{y\}=y-[y]$ for the fractional part.

**An integer sequence.** $\alpha$ and $1-\sqrt3=-\beta$ are the roots of $t^2-2t-2=0$. Hence $s_n=\alpha^n+(-\beta)^n$ satisfies $s_{n+2}=2s_{n+1}+2s_n$ with $s_0=2$, $s_1=2$, so every $s_n$ is an integer. (Alternatively: in the binomial expansions of $(\sqrt3+1)^n$ and $(1-\sqrt3)^n$ the odd powers of $\sqrt3$ cancel.)

**Even $n$.** Then $\alpha^n=s_n-\beta^n$ with $s_n\in\mathbb Z$ and $0<\beta^n<1$, so $[\alpha^n]=s_n-1$ and
$$\{\alpha^n\}=1-\beta^n\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1 .$$

**Odd $n$.** Then $\alpha^n=s_n+\beta^n$, so $[\alpha^n]=s_n$ and
$$\{\alpha^n\}=\beta^n\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0 .$$

The subsequence of even indices tends to $1$, that of odd indices to $0$. Therefore the limit **does not exist**. ∎

solutions.title: Numerical check

prompt: Let $f(x)$ be an even, twice continuously differentiable function and $f''(0)\ne0$. Prove that there is an extremum of $f(x)$ at the point $x=0$.
answer: Evenness gives $f'(0)=0$ (the one-sided difference quotients at $0$ are negatives of each other); then $f''(0)\ne0$ and the second-derivative test (Taylor with $f''$ continuous) give a strict extremum.

solutions.title: $f'(0)=0$, then the second-derivative test
solutions.body:
**Step 1: $f'(0)=0$.** Since $f$ is differentiable at $0$,
$$f'(0)=\lim_{h\to0^+}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h}=\lim_{h\to0^+}\frac{f(-h)-f(0)}{-h}.$$
Because $f(-h)=f(h)$, the second quotient is the negative of the first, so $f'(0)=-f'(0)$, i.e. $f'(0)=0$.

(Equivalently: differentiating $f(x)=f(-x)$ gives $f'(x)=-f'(-x)$, so $f'$ is odd and $f'(0)=0$.)

**Step 2: the sign of $f(x)-f(0)$.** Say $f''(0)>0$ (the case $f''(0)<0$ is symmetric). As $f''$ is continuous, there is $\delta>0$ with $f''(t)>0$ for $|t|<\delta$. For $0<|x|<\delta$, Taylor's formula with Lagrange remainder gives some $\xi$ between $0$ and $x$ with
$$f(x)=f(0)+f'(0)x+\tfrac12 f''(\xi)x^2=f(0)+\tfrac12 f''(\xi)x^2>f(0).$$
So $f$ has a strict local minimum at $0$. If $f''(0)<0$ the same argument gives $f(x)<f(0)$ for $0<|x|<\delta$, a strict local maximum.

Either way $f$ has an extremum at $x=0$. ∎
